questions.question: A team wants to make sure Claude never force-pushes to a shared branch. Per the CLAUDE.md/Skills/Hooks three-way split, which mechanism actually guarantees this, and why not just add a CLAUDE.md rule?
options: A hook — because CLAUDE.md and skills are instructions Claude *follows* and can still be skipped/forgotten, while a hook is code that *runs* and can outright block the action
CLAUDE.md — since it's the highest-priority instruction surface and is never overridden
A Skill, since skills automate any repeated procedure including safety rules
None of these are needed — the model's own judgment about danger is sufficient

questions.question: A team converts every project convention (formatting style, commit message format, and 'never touch prod') into hooks 'for maximum reliability.' What's the problem with this approach?
options: It over-applies hard enforcement to low-risk conventions that a CLAUDE.md rule or skill would handle fine — enforcement should be matched to actual risk, not maximized everywhere
Hooks cannot enforce formatting or commit conventions at all, only safety rules
There's no downside; more hooks is strictly better regardless of what they enforce
Hooks are slower than prompts so this always causes performance problems

questions.question: What's the distinguishing purpose of Skills versus CLAUDE.md versus Hooks?
options: CLAUDE.md = conventions that always apply; Skills = procedures/reference tied to a specific kind of task; Hooks = rules Claude must not be able to skip
They're three names for the same mechanism with different file extensions
CLAUDE.md only applies in CI; Skills and Hooks only apply interactively
Skills are for safety-critical rules, Hooks are for optional conventions

questions.question: In auto permission mode, what does the classifier actually guard against?
options: Intent that escalates beyond the request (e.g. production deploys, force-pushes, piping downloaded code into a shell) — not whether the code is correct
Both correctness and safety equally
Only correctness (e.g. broken logic), not safety
Nothing — auto mode has no classifier, it accepts everything unconditionally

questions.question: Why should auto mode always be paired with a stop hook that runs tests?
options: Because the classifier only blocks dangerous actions, not wrong ones — a broken refactor isn't dangerous so it passes the classifier, and only a test-running hook can catch that it's wrong
Because auto mode disables all hooks by default and stop hooks are the only ones that still fire
Because stop hooks are required to even enter auto mode
Auto mode doesn't need a stop hook if bypassPermissions is also enabled

questions.question: What does a hook exiting with code 2 do?
options: Blocking error — stderr is fed back to Claude as context, blocking almost everywhere; on 'stop' specifically it means 'not done yet'
Success — stdout JSON is parsed and applied
Non-blocking warning that's logged but ignored
Same as exit 1 — an error that does not block anything

questions.question: How should the level of verification scale with a Claude Code run's autonomy?
options: In proportion to autonomy — a short supervised session needs a glance, an unattended run or CI job needs a real check, since no one saw it happen
Verification effort should be constant regardless of how autonomous the run was
Only unattended runs need any verification at all; supervised sessions need none
Verification should scale with how long the run took, not how autonomous it was

questions.question: Which permission mode fits a CI pipeline where no one is present to approve actions, auto-denying anything not pre-approved?
options: dontAsk
acceptEdits
bypassPermissions
manual
